source.authors: Robert Sigl, Sebastian Steibl, Christian Laforsch
source.title: The role of vision for navigation in the crown-of-thorns seastar, Acanthaster planci

method: light microscopy of dissected compound eyes of arm tips; the Results give the average angle between the optical axes of neighbouring ommatidia
conditions: Wild adults collected around Moorea, French Polynesia, and kept without food in plastic bins with running seawater for 2-4 weeks before use (Methods, Experimental animals and area). Nine adults supplied one arm tip each; the Methods say one small (about 15 cm diameter) and four large (30-50 cm diameter) dissected eyes were used for the visual-field approximation, and the paper does not restate in the Results sentence how many eyes the average rests on. 11.2 ± 5.9 deg (± not defined as SD or SE); the following Results sentence says the angle varies across the eye, from dense areas to dispersed areas, so 11.2 deg is an eye-wide average, not a local value: the printed span runs from as little as 3.2 deg in dense areas to as much as 29.9 deg in dispersed areas. Main already holds an interommatidial_deg of approximately 8 deg for this species from another paper (Petie, Garm and Hall 2016, Frontiers in Zoology 13: 41, 10.1186/s12983-016-0174-9). Large individuals had 192-268 ommatidia per eye.
where: Results, Spatial resolution and visual field of the compound eye
quote: The average distance of the optical axes of neighbouring ommatidia is 11.2 ± 5.9°.
note: New-to-main value for this species; interommatidial_deg is a trait key already on main. Whole Results sentence (14 words), read intact in a second pass with its neighbours (the sentence before and after it were seen only in truncated form, which does not affect this sentence). Value is the sentence's mean; the ± term is kept in conditions. source.authors: Robert Sigl, Sebastian Steibl, Christian Laforsch
source.title: The role of vision for navigation in the crown-of-thorns seastar, Acanthaster planci

method: semi-thin sections of embedded eyes; acceptance angle of single ommatidia derived from the sectioned ommatidial structure (the Results sentence gives the minimum and maximum)
conditions: Wild adults collected around Moorea, French Polynesia, and kept without food in plastic bins with running seawater for 2-4 weeks before use (Methods, Experimental animals and area). Four eyes were embedded for semi-thin sectioning to analyse the acceptance angles (Methods, Spatial resolution and visual field). The two numbers are the mean minimum (17 ± 4 deg) and mean maximum (35 ± 9 deg) acceptance angle of the single ommatidia within the eye, so the range spans positions in the eye and is not a range between animals; ± not defined as SD or SE. The preceding Results sentence gives ommatidia 53 ± 12 um long and 16 ± 3 um wide.
where: Results, Spatial resolution and visual field of the compound eye
quote: They have a minimum acceptance angle of 17 ± 4° and a maximum acceptance angle of 35 ± 9°.
note: New-to-main value for this species and trait (acceptance_deg is a key already on main). Whole Results sentence (17 words); 'They' refers to the ommatidia named in the sentence before it ('The ommatidia themselves are 53 ± 12 μm long and 16 ± 3 μm wide.'), read in a second pass. Value is the two means in the sentence as a [minimum, maximum] pair. source.authors: Robert Sigl, Sebastian Steibl, Christian Laforsch
source.title: The role of vision for navigation in the crown-of-thorns seastar, Acanthaster planci

value: in field release trials, non-blinded adults found a reef structure significantly more often than blinded adults from 2.5 m and 5 m
method: field release experiment at Temae beach: one blinded (terminal ossicle with optic cushion removed) and one non-blinded adult placed together at a start point downstream of a reef structure, 1.25, 2.5, 5 and 10 m away; success = reaching the structure; Fisher's exact test
conditions: Wild adults collected around Moorea, French Polynesia, and kept without food in plastic bins with running seawater for 2-4 weeks before use (Methods, Experimental animals and area). N = 10 trials per distance except 11 at 5 m (each trial one blinded and one non-blinded animal); one blinded animal at 2.5 m excluded after a pufferfish attack. Both groups moved with the prevailing current in a preliminary test and displacement did not differ (one-way ANOVA F1,8 = 0.052, p > 0.05; n = 5 trials). Nulls: at 1.25 m more non-blinded animals found the structure but the difference was not significant (p = 0.070); at 10 m eyesight did not significantly increase success (p = 0.105), although 30% of non-blinded animals still found it. Pooled across distances the vision effect was reported as p < 0.001. Blinded animals moved downstream at 2.5 m and beyond. The Methods do not describe randomisation of treatment or trial order. Blinded animals had the eyes removed under 3.5% magnesium chloride anaesthesia and recovered only until the next day; no sham-operated or anaesthetised sighted control is described, so surgery and anaesthesia are confounded with eye loss. In each trial the blinded and the non-blinded animal were placed next to each other and released together. Per-distance success percentages are in Table 1. Field Nov-Dec 2013; tested animals had been kept unfed for 2-4 weeks.
where: Results, Field experiments, Experiment on visual navigation
quote: From a distance of 2.5 m and 5 m, non-blinded A. planci found the reef structure significantly more often than blinded A. planci (Fisher's exact test; p = 0.002 and p = 0.045, respectively).
note: Whole Results sentence (33 words), read intact in two abutting pieces ('From a distance of 2.5 m and 5 m, non-blinded A. planci found the reef structure significantly more often' | 'than blinded A. planci (Fisher's exact test; p = 0.002 and p = 0.045, respectively).'), final period seen. Value restates the quote; the two nulls (1.25 m, 10 m) and the pooled result from neighbouring Results sentences sit in conditions (value trimmed to the quote, audit 341). Eyed-animal vision test filed under behaviour_vision per rules; vision effect assessed by eye ablation, not by a stimulus series. value: 76.9% of eyeless adults (eyestalks removed) responded to white light with tail-flipping, walking or swimming; all eyed adults responded

source.authors: Mary W. Donohue, Jonathan H. Cohen, Thomas W. Cronin
source.title: Cerebral photoreception in mantis shrimp

method: behavioural trial: animals dark-adapted for 1 h, then exposed for 2 min to white light from a flood lamp (no wavelength or intensity given for the behavioural light); tail-flipping, walking or swimming scored from video (an infrared light illuminated the aquarium throughout dark adaptation and trials); eyes removed at the eyestalk base at least 24 h before testing
conditions: Neogonodactylus oerstedii from the Florida Keys (the paper does not say who collected or supplied them, or when; no rearing is described), kept in plastic aquaria of about 800 ml artificial seawater on 12 h light:12 h dark. The paper gives no group sizes for eyed or eyeless animals, light or dark (not in the text, Methods or Figure 2 legend), so the percentages have no stated denominator. Dark controls of equal duration: the next Results sentence gives 25.0% (eyed) and 27.3% (eyeless) showing any of these behaviours in the dark, and says the light values were significantly greater than both; the Methods say significance between treatments was determined by chi-square analyses. Response latency was longer for eyeless animals (6.7 s eyed vs 26.5 s eyeless; Mann-Whitney U, P<0.05). The cerebral photoreceptor the paper records from is a pigmented putative ventral (median) eye on the cerebral ganglion, which eyestalk removal leaves in place; recorded extracellularly in eyeless animals (n = 2-5 flashes per preparation, three preparations), it responded within 31 ms (±12 ms sd) of a 500 ms white xenon flash. Eyeless animals are a surgical preparation, not a natural state; the behavioural responses were not localised to the ventral eye, and the authors say currently undescribed non-cerebral photoreceptors may elicit them; the eyed value is 'all' with no n stated.
where: Results, Evidence for functional extraocular photoreceptors
quote: All eyed mantis shrimp showed one or more of these responses, whereas 76.9% of eyeless mantis shrimp responded according to our criteria (Fig. 2).
note: Whole Results sentence (25 words) read intact in two abutting pieces ('All eyed mantis shrimp showed one or more of these responses,' | 'whereas 76.9% of eyeless mantis shrimp responded according to our criteria (Fig. 2).'), final period seen; trailing figure reference kept inside the quote. 'These responses' = tail-flipping, walking, swimming as defined in Methods. Trait sense_light_nonvisual used for light detection without the compound eyes, which the authors call extraocular 'nonvisual' photoreception; the receptor they record from is a putative ventral (median) eye on the cerebral ganglion (key exists on main; audit 341). Family Gonodactylidae and order Stomatopoda from OBIS (taxonID 408949, accepted, (Hansen, 1895); audit 341); main's gaps/try-species.json leaves family blank for this species. Name Neogonodactylus oerstedii EXACT ACCEPTED in main's docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (Gonodactylus oerstedii is its SYNONYM; the paper uses the accepted name). Main holds only eye_movement rows for this species (10.1098/rstb.2013.0042); s41598-018-28004 appears nowhere in docs/, desk-d23*/d24* evidence or unit branches. source.authors: Jérôme Delroisse, Jérôme Mallefet, Patrick Flammang
source.title: De Novo Adult Transcriptomes of Two European Brittle Stars: Spotlight on Opsin-Based Photoreception

method: de novo assembly of an adult arm-tissue transcriptome and search for opsin transcripts (reciprocal BLAST and phylogenetic placement); the three transcripts are named in the quote
conditions: Wild-collected Amphiura filiformis (mud grab, 25-40 m, Lovén Center, Kristineberg, Sweden, November 2012). Arm tissue from 3 individuals was pooled for RNA extraction, so the count is for the pooled transcriptome, not per animal. The transcripts are partial (the paper's Conclusion says partial opsin transcripts for three genes were detected). The same paper notes 13 opsin genes had been identified earlier in a draft A. filiformis genome, so 3 is the number detected in this adult arm transcriptome, not the species' opsin gene count. The quoted sentence cites the paper's reference 29 for the three opsins, and the sentence before it says this transcriptome was also previously screened for the presence of opsins, so the three were first reported in that earlier screen. The paper also reports two opsins for Ophiopsila aranea (not filed here: that sentence is over 40 words).
where: Results and Discussion, Candidate opsin transcripts in O. aranea
quote: Three opsin mRNAs were discovered in the adult transcriptome of A. filiformis [29]: one r-opsin (Af-opsin 4.5), one neuropsin (Af-opsin 8.2), and one basal-branch opsin (Af-opsin 2) [29].
note: New trait: opsin_sequences_recovered is a key already on main (oa-1 rows) though absent from the checker list. Whole Results sentence (28 words with its two [29] reference markers, which the quote carries; audit 341), read intact in two abutting pieces ('Three opsin mRNAs ... one r-opsin (Af-opsin 4.5),' | 'one neuropsin (Af-opsin 8.2), and one basal-branch opsin (Af-opsin 2).'), final period seen; it sits under the subsection headed for O. aranea on the page, so 'where' follows that heading. Family Amphiuridae and order Amphilepidida from OBIS (api.obis.org/v3/taxon, taxonID 125080, accepted, (O.F. Müller, 1776); audit 341); neither is stated in the paper and main holds no Amphiura row. Amphiura filiformis appears in a search-result OBIS title as 'Amphiura filiformis (O.F. Müller, 1776)'; it is not in main's gbif-names.tsv; OBIS gives it as accepted, not a synonym (audit 341). No Amphiura or Ophiopsila row and no pone.0152988 anywhere in docs/, desk-d23*/d24* evidence or unit branches.
